explanations.answer: Don't leave out a single word
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The LORD tells Jeremiah, "Do not omit a word." (Jeremiah 26:2) Every word stays in. Skip the chocolate chips and that's not the recipe anymore. Jeremiah doesn't get to trim the message.

The LORD never says anything about how many times. His instruction is about the words themselves: "Do not omit a word." (Jeremiah 26:2) So the message goes out whole, with nothing cut. Easy to mix up when you're thinking about how much to say instead of what to say.

explanations.answer: Write it on a scroll first
explanations.explanation: No scroll shows up in this part of the story. The LORD says, "Stand in the courtyard of the house of the LORD and speak all the words I have commanded you to speak…" (Jeremiah 26:2) Jeremiah's job here is to stand and say it out loud. And the one extra instruction is, "Do not omit a word."

I get why it sounds that way, with all that warning in the air. But the LORD actually says, "Perhaps they will listen and turn…" (Jeremiah 26:3) That word "perhaps" leaves the door open. A no-chance message wouldn't need a "perhaps" in it, baker.

Right, the LORD doesn't say there's no chance. He says, "Perhaps they will listen and turn…" (Jeremiah 26:3) The aim is that they turn from their evil way of life, so that He may relent of the disaster He is planning. Perhaps is a small word, but it's holding a big door open.

That's the word, friend. The LORD says He will make the city "…an object of cursing among all the nations of the earth." (Jeremiah 26:6) That's a heavy line. It's the picture of what's at stake if they won't listen.

Envy would mean the nations wished they had the city. The LORD says the opposite: "…an object of cursing among all the nations of the earth." (Jeremiah 26:6) Cursing, not envy. It's a sobering picture.

Praise would be a lovely ending, baker, but that's not what the LORD says here. He says the city would become "…an object of cursing among all the nations of the earth." (Jeremiah 26:6) That's what He says will happen if they won't listen. The warning is the whole point of the line.

explanations.answer: Seize him and shout for his death
explanations.explanation: Yes. The priests, the prophets and all the people seized him, shouting, "You must surely die!" (Jeremiah 26:8) This part of the story is heavy, and I think it hurts to read it. Jeremiah had just finished saying everything the LORD commanded, and it turned on him that fast.

explanations.answer: Tear their clothes and cry out
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't show anybody grieving here. They seized him and shouted, "You must surely die!" (Jeremiah 26:8) I think that's anger aimed straight at Jeremiah. It's a hard moment.

explanations.answer: Turn and walk out in silence
explanations.explanation: Nobody walks out quietly in this scene, friend. Right when Jeremiah finishes, the priests, the prophets and all the people seize him and shout, "You must surely die!" (Jeremiah 26:8) It's loud and it's fast. It's one of the heavier moments in the story.

That's what the crowd shouts. They say he dared to prophesy that "…this city will be desolate and deserted!" (Jeremiah 26:9) They say it right to his face. They repeat his message back at him, and I bet they are not happy about it.

Foreign kings never come up in the crowd's shout. They say he dared to prophesy that "…this city will be desolate and deserted!" (Jeremiah 26:9) A city under a foreign king still has people in it, baker. Desolate and deserted means nobody's home.

A split isn't what the crowd is yelling about here. Their words are, "…this city will be desolate and deserted!" (Jeremiah 26:9) I think they're upset that Jeremiah said it in the name of the LORD. Desolate and deserted is the answer.

explanations.answer: They heard it with their own ears
explanations.explanation: Exactly. The priests and prophets tell the officials and the people that they know it "…as you have heard with your own ears!" (Jeremiah 26:11) That's their claim. No middleman, just ears.

explanations.answer: The king read it out to them
explanations.explanation: The king isn't reading anything in this scene. The priests and prophets say, "…as you have heard with your own ears!" (Jeremiah 26:11) The officials did come up from the king's palace, but the priests and prophets point to hearing, not to the king.

explanations.answer: A scribe wrote it down for them
explanations.explanation: No scribe shows up in this scene, friend. The priests and prophets say to the officials and people, "…as you have heard with your own ears!" (Jeremiah 26:11) That's what the priests and prophets are claiming: hearing, not reading. No paperwork involved, just ears.

That's right, baker. The priests and prophets say the man is worthy of death "…for he has prophesied against this city…" (Jeremiah 26:11) That's the reason they give. Plain and simple, they point to what he said about the city.

It's true, friend, and the text says so. The priests and prophets give this reason: "…for he has prophesied against this city…" (Jeremiah 26:11) That's the charge they bring to the officials and the people. One reason, stated out loud.

explanations.answer: Correct their ways and obey the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Jeremiah says, "…correct your ways and deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God…" (Jeremiah 26:13) His own life is on the line and he's still urging them to turn. He keeps pointing the crowd back to the LORD instead of at himself.

explanations.answer: Let him go and forget his words
explanations.explanation: Jeremiah never asks to be let go. He says, "…correct your ways and deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God…" (Jeremiah 26:13) Right after that he says, "…here I am in your hands…" (Jeremiah 26:14) He wants them to listen, not forget.

explanations.answer: Take his case before the king
explanations.explanation: Jeremiah's talking to the officials and all the people, and he doesn't ask for the king. His plea is, "…correct your ways and deeds, and obey the voice of the LORD your God…" (Jeremiah 26:13) The king isn't part of his request. He's asking them to turn.

Yes, baker. Jeremiah says, "…you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves, upon this city, and upon its residents…" (Jeremiah 26:15) I think he's calm about it, even with a crowd around him. It's a serious warning.

The word isn't foreign. Jeremiah says, "…you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves, upon this city, and upon its residents…" (Jeremiah 26:15) He's talking about innocent blood. And it lands on them and on the city.

Royal blood isn't what Jeremiah is talking about, friend. He says, "…you will bring innocent blood upon yourselves, upon this city, and upon its residents…" (Jeremiah 26:15) Innocent is the word he picks. And it lands in three places: on them, on the city, and on the people living in it.

explanations.answer: This man is not worthy of death
explanations.explanation: That's it. The officials and all the people tell the priests and prophets, "This man is not worthy of death…" (Jeremiah 26:16) That's a big turn from the shouting earlier. And they say it straight to the priests and prophets.

explanations.answer: This man must leave the city
explanations.explanation: Nobody mentions sending him out of the city. The officials and the people say, "This man is not worthy of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God!" (Jeremiah 26:16) That's the verdict and the reason together. Nothing about banishing him.

explanations.answer: This man must face the king
explanations.explanation: The king isn't part of their answer here, baker. They say, "This man is not worthy of death, for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God!" (Jeremiah 26:16) That's what they tell the priests and prophets. Their reason is that he spoke to them in the name of the LORD their God.

explanations.answer: Zion will be plowed like a field
explanations.explanation: Right, friend. The elders say Micah told all Judah, "Zion will be plowed like a field…" (Jeremiah 26:18) Micah the Moreshite was a prophet in the days of Hezekiah, king of Judah. He gave a hard message too, and the elders bring it up on purpose.

explanations.answer: Zion will never be shaken again
explanations.explanation: That's the opposite of what the elders quote. They say Micah told the people, "Zion will be plowed like a field…" (Jeremiah 26:18) Plowed like a field is a long way from never shaken. It was a hard word from Micah the Moreshite.

explanations.answer: Zion will be crowned with glory
explanations.explanation: Glory would be nicer to hear, baker. But the elders quote Micah as saying, "Zion will be plowed like a field…" (Jeremiah 26:18) Micah the Moreshite brought a hard message. That's the one the elders quote.

Not quite, friend. The elders ask, "Did Hezekiah king of Judah or anyone else in Judah put him to death?" (Jeremiah 26:19) Nothing in the text has Hezekiah putting Micah to death. Instead the elders say Hezekiah feared the LORD and sought His favor.

That's right, baker. The elders ask, "Did Hezekiah king of Judah or anyone else in Judah put him to death?" (Jeremiah 26:19) Nothing in the text has anyone putting Micah to death. The elders say Hezekiah feared the LORD and sought His favor.

Yes. The elders finish with, "But we are about to bring great harm on ourselves!" (Jeremiah 26:19) They look at what they're about to do and say it out loud. I think that's a brave thing to say to a crowd.
The elders do say it, friend. Their last line is, "But we are about to bring great harm on ourselves!" (Jeremiah 26:19) That's their warning to the whole assembly. They don't hold back.
That's right, baker. The text says, "…the king sought to put him to death." (Jeremiah 26:21) King Jehoiakim and his mighty men and officials heard Uriah's words. It's a heavy part of the story.
Prison isn't what the king is after here. The text says, "…the king sought to put him to death." (Jeremiah 26:21) That's what Jehoiakim tried to do. It's a heavy moment.

A cistern doesn't show up in this part of the story, friend. The text says, "…the king sought to put him to death." (Jeremiah 26:21) That's what the king was after. It's a serious moment, and the text keeps it short.
Yes, baker. The text says, "…he fled in fear and went to Egypt." (Jeremiah 26:21) Uriah son of Shemaiah heard what the king wanted and ran. I think anyone would feel that kind of fear.
The text doesn't say anger. It says, "…he fled in fear and went to Egypt." (Jeremiah 26:21) Uriah found out the king sought to put him to death, and he fled. The word the text picks is fear.
Shame isn't the word the text uses, friend. It says Uriah "…fled in fear and went to Egypt." (Jeremiah 26:21) He found out what the king wanted, and he ran. Fear is the answer.

That's the name, baker. The text says, "Nevertheless, Ahikam son of Shaphan supported Jeremiah, so he was not handed over to the people to be put to death." (Jeremiah 26:24) Everybody needs somebody on their side when the room turns cold. For Jeremiah, that was Ahikam.

Seraiah son of Neriah isn't named in this passage. The person who supports Jeremiah is "…Ahikam son of Shaphan…" (Jeremiah 26:24) Because of that support, Jeremiah was not handed over to the people to be put to death. Keep Ahikam's name in your pocket.

Pashhur son of Immer doesn't show up in this passage, friend. The text says, "…Ahikam son of Shaphan supported Jeremiah…" (Jeremiah 26:24) That support kept Jeremiah from being handed over to the people to be put to death. So Ahikam is the answer.
